questions.question: Why is a happy-path output test insufficient for an agent skill?
questions.answer: It can miss incorrect triggering, unsafe execution paths, regressions with other skills, and excessive context cost.
questions.explanation: A correct answer from one isolated run does not establish that the skill behaves reliably in the full library.

questions.question: A support skill passes its own tests but starts ignoring account-security instructions when co-loaded with other skills. Which coverage condition failed?
questions.answer: Regression coverage failed.
questions.explanation: Regression coverage checks that a skill remains compatible with the wider library and does not degrade neighboring behavior.

questions.question: What is the correct three-layer order for progressive skill disclosure?
options: Metadata, instruction body, then resources as needed
Resources, metadata, then instruction body
All instructions and resources on every turn
Instruction body only
questions.answer: Metadata, instruction body, then resources as needed
questions.explanation: Short metadata supports routing; full instructions load on activation; bundled material loads only when required.

questions.question: Why not load every skill's full instructions into every agent turn?
questions.answer: It wastes tokens and dilutes the task-relevant context.
questions.explanation: The approach keeps a large library discoverable while limiting active context to the relevant procedure and resources.

questions.question: An agent receives a request to summarize a PDF. What should progressive disclosure load first?
questions.answer: The relevant skill's metadata is already visible; after routing selects the PDF skill, load its instruction body, then only the needed PDF tools or references.
questions.explanation: Each layer is introduced only when the task requires it, preserving context budget.

questions.question: How should an installed agent skill be treated?
options: As a versioned software dependency
As harmless documentation
As a prompt that cannot affect tools
As an automatically trusted update
questions.answer: As a versioned software dependency
questions.explanation: Skills can include executable code and operational instructions, so adoption needs normal dependency discipline.

questions.question: Name two controls for adopting a third-party skill.
questions.answer: Any two of trusted-source checks, version pinning, code review, security scanning, assigned ownership, and regression testing.
questions.explanation: These controls establish provenance and make changes inspectable and reversible.

questions.question: A community skill update adds a new shell script and asks for production credentials. What should the team do before updating?
questions.answer: Keep the version pinned until the update is reviewed and scanned, test it with narrow staging access, and approve it through the owned change process.
questions.explanation: New executable behavior and increased privilege require fresh provenance, review, and least-privilege checks.

questions.question: What kind of memory does an agent skill primarily provide?
options: Reusable task procedure
A raw chat transcript
A model weight update
Only factual reference data
questions.answer: Reusable task procedure
questions.explanation: Skills package step-by-step know-how that an agent can load when a task needs it.

questions.question: Why are skills useful even when a model already knows relevant facts?
questions.answer: They preserve a reviewed multi-step workflow so the agent does not have to reconstruct it from scratch each time.
questions.explanation: Knowing facts is different from reliably executing a repeated procedure.

questions.question: A team repeatedly asks agents to prepare release notes using the same approved checks. What should it create?
questions.answer: A reusable release-note skill containing the reviewed procedure and any needed scripts or references.
questions.explanation: The skill turns a successful repeated workflow into portable procedural memory.

questions.question: Which authority ladder is recommended for agent skills?
options: Read-only, draft-only, action-allowed
Administrator, editor, viewer
Offline, online, autonomous
Prompt, tool, model
questions.answer: Read-only, draft-only, action-allowed
questions.explanation: The ladder grows authority gradually as evidence and review rigor increase.

questions.question: Why should action-allowed skills have a higher release threshold than read-only skills?
questions.answer: Their mistakes can mutate real systems and cause greater or irreversible harm.
questions.explanation: Greater authority increases the cost of failure, so stronger evidence and approvals are required.

questions.question: A new payroll skill has correct output tests but no audited tool traces or security approval. What tier should it have?
questions.answer: At most draft-only, not action-allowed.
questions.explanation: A consequential mutation needs stronger execution evidence and review than correct output alone provides.

questions.question: What should happen to a skill change proposed by a meta-skill?
options: Enter the draft tier and clear evaluation and review
Become action-allowed immediately
Replace the whole library
Be trusted if the meta-skill is confident
questions.answer: Enter the draft tier and clear evaluation and review
questions.explanation: Generated changes are not exempt from ordinary promotion gates.

questions.question: What risk do evaluation gates prevent in self-improving skill libraries?
questions.answer: They prevent unreviewed changes from gaming metrics, breaking routing or neighboring skills, and expanding a weak library automatically.
questions.explanation: Gates make generated improvements prove their value and safety before deployment.

questions.question: A meta-skill sees one successful trace and proposes a new payment skill. What is the safe next step?
questions.answer: Keep the proposal as a draft, add representative evaluations, and require human review before granting any action authority.
questions.explanation: One successful trace is evidence for a candidate, not a reason to deploy a new consequential capability.

questions.question: What should a skill description include besides what the skill does?
options: When to use it and when not to use it
Its full implementation
All possible tool output
A promise of perfect accuracy
questions.answer: When to use it and when not to use it
questions.explanation: Concrete triggers and anti-triggers make the description a reliable routing contract.

questions.question: Why can a vague skill description cause regressions?
questions.answer: It can route unrelated requests to the skill, adding irrelevant context and interfering with other skills.
questions.explanation: Descriptions select what instructions enter the active context, so overlap creates false activations.

questions.question: A skill says only 'use for data tasks' and activates for a request to summarize a dashboard. What should be added?
questions.answer: Concrete positive triggers and an explicit non-trigger saying it is not for summarization or read-only analysis.
questions.explanation: Specific boundaries let routing distinguish the intended task from superficially similar work.

questions.question: Why are skills a useful unit of agent improvement?
options: They are conditional, versioned, and owned
They always replace the model
They load into every prompt
They need no tests
questions.answer: They are conditional, versioned, and owned
questions.explanation: A skill bounds the change and activation surface, making it independently testable and maintainable.

questions.question: What is the context cost of improving behavior through a global system prompt?
questions.answer: Every task pays for the extra instructions, including unrelated tasks that can also regress.
questions.explanation: A conditional skill limits its context cost and behavior change to tasks where it activates.

questions.question: A team needs better invoice extraction but does not want to change every support interaction. What should it do?
questions.answer: Create and version a narrowly triggered invoice-extraction skill with its own tests and owner.
questions.explanation: The skill improves the specific capability without imposing global-prompt cost or broad regression risk.

questions.question: Where should a multi-skill workflow keep its durable intermediate state?
options: In structured files, schemas, or a message bus
Only in accumulated chat context
In an unvalidated prose summary
Only in model weights
questions.answer: In structured files, schemas, or a message bus
questions.explanation: External structured state makes handoffs inspectable, reproducible, and independent of context-window limits.

questions.question: Why should an LLM context window not be used as a workflow database?
questions.answer: It obscures state, compounds errors through raw outputs, consumes attention, and makes runs difficult to reproduce or debug.
questions.explanation: Structured external artifacts let each step inspect and validate a stable handoff.

questions.question: A research skill sends paragraphs of notes directly into a writer skill, causing lost citations. What should the workflow change?
questions.answer: Write a validated structured artifact containing claims and citations, then have the writer consume that artifact.
questions.explanation: The structured handoff preserves state and gives later steps a debuggable, reproducible source of truth.

questions.question: Which role in the agentic security response triad detects unusual execution behavior?
options: Red
Blue
Green
Yellow
questions.answer: Blue
questions.explanation: Blue agents baseline normal paths and detect anomalies.

questions.question: What does the Green role preserve while quarantining a compromised agent?
questions.answer: Its short-term state or memory for forensic analysis.
questions.explanation: Green stops external action while retaining evidence needed to investigate and repair the workflow.

questions.question: A release agent begins calling an unapproved deployment tool. What should the triad do?
questions.answer: Blue detects the deviation; Green revokes the agent's tool access, preserves evidence, and repairs the workflow; Red can add the case as a future probe.
questions.explanation: The roles divide proactive testing, detection, and state-preserving containment and repair.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a Vibe Diff before a high-stakes action?
options: Compress logs
Translate the proposed action into plain language tied to user intent
Grant broad admin access
Replace MFA
questions.answer: Translate the proposed action into plain language tied to user intent
questions.explanation: A Vibe Diff helps the reviewer understand what they are authorizing rather than rubber-stamping code.

questions.question: Why are simple approve/deny buttons unsafe for high-stakes generated actions?
questions.answer: They create confirmation fatigue and can make people approve syntax or side effects they do not understand.
questions.explanation: Approval must be informed and specific, not a repeated reflex.

questions.question: An agent says a command will remove test rows, but its Vibe Diff reveals it deletes an entire production table. What should happen?
questions.answer: Do not approve it; require a scoped action that matches the user's intent.
questions.explanation: The intent-to-action explanation exposes the mismatch before authorization.

questions.question: Effective trust is best described as what?
options: A one-time deployment check
A continuously updated runtime authorization judgment
A static password policy
A model benchmark score
questions.answer: A continuously updated runtime authorization judgment
questions.explanation: It incorporates current identity, behavior, tools, data, supply chain, and task context.

questions.question: Why is a valid credential insufficient evidence that an agent should continue acting?
questions.answer: It proves a past identity check, not that the agent still follows the authorized intent or behaves safely now.
questions.explanation: Non-deterministic agents can drift or be compromised after authentication.

questions.question: A documentation agent asks for a production database credential. How should effective-trust controls respond?
questions.answer: Treat it as context and intent drift, block or narrow the action, and require review.
questions.explanation: The new resource request is outside its authorized task and lowers effective trust.

questions.question: What happens to state in an ephemeral agent sandbox after its task?
options: It is reset or destroyed
It is copied to the host
It becomes the next task's workspace
It gains network access
questions.answer: It is reset or destroyed
questions.explanation: Ephemeral sandboxes prevent compromised logic from persisting between runs.

questions.question: Name two restrictions an agent execution sandbox should enforce.
questions.answer: Any two of restricted host access, network isolation, limited files, and state reset between runs.
questions.explanation: Isolation limits the blast radius of untrusted generated code.

questions.question: An agent must test a generated install script. What is the safe execution setup?
questions.answer: Run it in a new isolated sandbox with only required files and narrow network access, then destroy it after collecting results.
questions.explanation: This makes a failed or malicious script unable to persist or affect the host.

questions.question: What is slopsquatting?
options: Publishing malware under a package name hallucinated by a model
Deleting old dependencies
Using a package lockfile
Scanning a container image
questions.answer: Publishing malware under a package name hallucinated by a model
questions.explanation: Attackers can claim invented names that an agent may later try to install.

questions.question: Give two controls that defend against hallucinated-package slopsquatting.
questions.answer: Any two of vetted registries, exact version pinning, SBOM verification, signature checks, and CI authorization gates.
questions.explanation: These controls establish provenance before a dependency reaches production.

questions.question: An agent proposes a package missing from the approved internal registry. What should CI do?
questions.answer: Reject the unverified dependency and require a reviewed, provenance-checked addition or an approved alternative.
questions.explanation: An absent package may be model-invented and unsafe to fetch blindly from a public registry.

questions.question: Why is one passing unit test insufficient to evaluate a coding agent?
options: It cannot reveal every quality dimension
Unit tests are always wrong
It prevents code execution
It costs too little
questions.answer: It cannot reveal every quality dimension
questions.explanation: A passing test can still hide intent, visual, cost, convention, trajectory, and repair failures.

questions.question: Name three dimensions of multidimensional coding-agent evaluation.
questions.answer: Any three of intent satisfaction, functional correctness, visual and behavioral correctness, efficiency, convention fit, trajectory quality, and self-repair.
questions.explanation: Different dimensions need different complementary methods.

questions.question: A checkout page passes payment tests but has inaccessible controls and used an unapproved payment tool. What evidence should be added?
questions.answer: Browser or accessibility checks plus trace inspection, alongside the existing functional tests.
questions.explanation: Those methods cover visual behavior and trajectory quality that payment tests miss.

questions.question: What does a Runtime Agent Bill of Materials inventory?
options: Active models, tools, data sources, credentials, and associations
Only source-code files
Only model weights
Only static package dependencies
questions.answer: Active models, tools, data sources, credentials, and associations
questions.explanation: An AgBOM maps the live resources affecting an agent's current blast radius.

questions.question: Why is a static inventory inadequate for an agent?
questions.answer: Agents can dynamically discover tools, data, and subgoals, making a static list stale during execution.
questions.explanation: A live inventory exposes the current blast radius and possible intent drift.

questions.question: A research agent requests a CRM connector midway through a task. How should an AgBOM help?
questions.answer: Record the connector and credential immediately so trust controls can flag or stop the out-of-scope expansion.
questions.explanation: The live inventory makes the new resource and its blast-radius effect visible.

questions.question: What is the central question of session convergence evaluation?
options: Was one turn grammatically correct?
Did the user reach an accepted result?
Was the model the largest?
Did the session have exactly two turns?
questions.answer: Did the user reach an accepted result?
questions.explanation: It evaluates the whole multi-turn interaction, not isolated replies.

questions.question: Name two measurements besides the final result that session convergence tracks.
questions.answer: Any two of corrections or turns to converge, cost to converge, and abandonment.
questions.explanation: These reveal whether a locally plausible answer produced a useful overall experience.

questions.question: A user abandons an agent after six corrections although an early reply passed a unit test. How should the session be classified?
questions.answer: As an informative non-converged failure, and the corrections should become labeled evaluation data.
questions.explanation: Session-level evidence overrides the misleading success of one isolated response.

questions.question: What is the underspecification gap?
options: The distance between an incomplete request and unstated requirements
A network latency metric
A model context-window limit
A package-version mismatch
questions.answer: The distance between an incomplete request and unstated requirements
questions.explanation: An agent must infer this hidden specification to satisfy user intent.

questions.question: Why can functional correctness fail to establish intent satisfaction?
questions.answer: A prompt may omit aesthetic, operational, accessibility, and project-specific expectations that a functional test does not cover.
questions.explanation: The agent can pass a narrow test while missing the user's unstated requirements.

questions.question: A user asks for a clean filter panel; the result works but breaks keyboard focus and project styling. What evaluation is needed?
questions.answer: Evaluate against an inferred intent rubric that includes accessibility and project conventions, not only functional tests.
questions.explanation: The request's hidden acceptance criteria define the underspecification gap.

questions.question: Zero ambient authority means an agent should receive what?
options: The developer's permanent admin token
Only short-lived credentials scoped to the task
A shared production password
No identity at all
questions.answer: Only short-lived credentials scoped to the task
questions.explanation: The credential should match the exact user, intent, resources, and time window.

questions.question: What problem does zero ambient authority prevent when an agent is prompt-injected?
questions.answer: It prevents the agent from using broad inherited privileges as a confused deputy to access unrelated systems or secrets.
questions.explanation: Deny-by-default, task-scoped authority limits the damage of a confused agent.

questions.question: An agent must edit one staging file for fifteen minutes. What credential should it receive?
questions.answer: A fresh token that can write only that staging file for that task and expires after fifteen minutes.
questions.explanation: Just-in-time downscoping makes authority specific to user intent, resource, and time.

questions.question: Where should a repository-wide test command normally live?
options: In the current chat only
In a project instruction file such as AGENTS.md
In each task's temporary note
In every individual skill
questions.answer: In a project instruction file such as AGENTS.md
questions.explanation: A stable repository convention needs a durable, project-wide home rather than a session-specific instruction.

questions.question: What determines the best home for an agent instruction?
questions.answer: Its lifetime and audience.
questions.explanation: Use the narrowest durable layer that reaches the people or agents who need the rule for as long as they need it.

questions.question: A team repeatedly asks agents to update the changelog whenever code changes. Where should that instruction go?
questions.answer: In a reusable agent skill.
questions.explanation: The procedure applies across tasks but is more specific than a global or project identity rule, making a reusable skill the appropriate scope.

questions.question: What is the main risk of frequent low-value approval prompts?
options: Agents become deterministic
Reviewers begin rubber-stamping them
Tests stop running
Project files become read-only
questions.answer: Reviewers begin rubber-stamping them
questions.explanation: Constant micro-approvals deplete attention and can turn human review into reflexive clicking.

questions.question: How should an agent approval system preserve human attention?
questions.answer: Automate bounded low-risk work and use risk-triggered checkpoints for consequential or out-of-bound actions.
questions.explanation: The goal is to reserve limited human attention for decisions where it adds real safety value.

questions.question: An agent requests approval for every formatting change and test run, but developers ignore production-permission alerts. What should the team change?
questions.answer: Allow the bounded routine actions automatically and reserve approvals for risky actions such as permission changes.
questions.explanation: Removing low-value prompts makes the remaining high-impact checkpoint more likely to receive real scrutiny.

questions.question: What is the primary role of an executable specification?
options: A disposable chat transcript
A versioned shared source of truth for implementation and verification
A replacement for all tests
A list of model parameters
questions.answer: A versioned shared source of truth for implementation and verification
questions.explanation: It gives humans and agents the durable requirements, contracts, constraints, and scenarios needed to build and check a system.

questions.question: Name two useful parts of an executable specification.
questions.answer: Any two of technical design, rationale and constraints, API contracts, diagrams, and behavioral scenarios.
questions.explanation: These details make intended architecture and verifiable behavior explicit rather than leaving gaps for an agent to guess.

questions.question: Before an agent builds payment retries, what should a team add to the specification to make success testable?
questions.answer: A concrete behavioral scenario with the starting state, action, expected result, and important edge cases.
questions.explanation: A Given/When/Then-style scenario supplies the behavior the agent should implement and the test should verify.

questions.question: What should a bug-fix prompt require before the agent edits code?
options: A style refactor
Reproducible evidence such as a failing test or command
A new project scaffold
An approval for every line
questions.answer: Reproducible evidence such as a failing test or command
questions.explanation: Evidence-first prompting lets the agent identify and repair the root cause, then keep a regression check.

questions.question: Why should agent prompts change with the execution mode?
questions.answer: Different task types need different evidence, constraints, and verification.
questions.explanation: New projects, features, bugs, documentation, and data work have materially different risks and success conditions.

questions.question: An agent is asked to add a feature to an existing service. What should its prompt emphasize?
questions.answer: Existing naming and error-handling conventions, the relevant specification, and a reviewable diff.
questions.explanation: Feature mode builds on an existing codebase, so matching local conventions and exposing the change are key controls.

questions.question: What must happen before a tool call runs in hybrid policy gating?
options: Only a semantic model review
Only a role check
Both structural authorization and semantic action review
A user approves every call
questions.answer: Both structural authorization and semantic action review
questions.explanation: Structural rules decide whether the tool is available, while semantic review checks whether the proposed use and arguments are safe.

questions.question: Why is structural gating alone insufficient for an agent tool call?
questions.answer: It can allow the tool but cannot recognize every unsafe intent or argument combination.
questions.explanation: A permitted tool can still be used in a way that violates a natural-language policy, so semantic review supplies a second check.

questions.question: An administrator is allowed to send email, but an agent proposes emailing unmasked customer records to a broad list. What should the policy gate do?
questions.answer: Reject or escalate the action through semantic gating before the email tool runs.
questions.explanation: The role passes structural authorization, but the proposed arguments can still violate privacy policy.

questions.question: In high-velocity code review, what should automated tooling handle?
options: Architecture trade-offs only
Mechanical checks such as style and routine tests
All product decisions
Human approval for every line
questions.answer: Mechanical checks such as style and routine tests
questions.explanation: Automation handles repeatable checks so reviewers can focus on behavior, architecture, and material risk.

questions.question: What should a high-velocity pull request summary tell a reviewer?
questions.answer: What changed, likely breakage points, and the associated risk.
questions.explanation: A concise risk summary lets scarce human attention go to the most consequential parts of a change.

questions.question: A reviewer has checked an API contract change but the required test suite is still running. What is a suitable high-velocity integration decision?
questions.answer: Give conditional approval that permits merging only after the required automated tests pass.
questions.explanation: Conditional approval avoids an unnecessary wait while retaining the test gate for the change.

questions.question: Which review tier is usually the practical starting point for a team that needs repository-specific review criteria but no cross-run memory?
options: Managed reviewer only
CI-hosted custom reviewer
Fully owned stateful reviewer
Manual review only
questions.answer: CI-hosted custom reviewer
questions.explanation: The middle tier lets the team own prompts and criteria while the CI provider owns the runtime; it avoids unnecessary stateful-runtime overhead.

questions.question: What three questions help select a continuous review runtime tier?
questions.answer: How specific the review criteria are, whether cross-run memory is needed, and how severe failure would be.
questions.explanation: These questions distinguish generic managed review from CI-hosted custom review and a fully owned stateful runtime.

questions.question: A managed reviewer misses a repository-specific privacy rule but has no need for cross-pull-request memory. What should the team try next?
questions.answer: A CI-triggered custom reviewer with a repository-owned privacy-review skill.
questions.explanation: Tier 2 supplies team-specific criteria without the cost and operating burden of a fully owned stateful reviewer.

questions.question: Which is the best first AI pilot?
options: An AI that approves customer refunds automatically
An AI that changes payroll records
An internal assistant that drafts IT-ticket summaries for review
An AI that controls production deployments
questions.answer: An internal assistant that drafts IT-ticket summaries for review
questions.explanation: It is narrow, internal, reversible, and reviewed, so a failure creates limited disruption.

questions.question: Why should an early AI pilot avoid mission-critical and customer-facing workflows?
questions.answer: Because early pilots have unknown failures, and limiting the scope prevents those failures from causing material harm while the team learns.
questions.explanation: A pilot is an experiment; its business impact should remain small and reversible.

questions.question: A bank wants to test an AI that writes loan-denial notices. How can it make the pilot risk-bounded?
questions.answer: Use it to prepare drafts for a small internal review team, require human approval, and keep the existing notice process as the fallback rather than sending notices automatically.
questions.explanation: The scope, audience, and consequences stay controlled while the team learns about quality and workflow fit.

questions.question: What is the best starting point for selecting an AI use case?
options: A newly released model feature
A specific business problem with measurable value
The largest department
The easiest demo to build
questions.answer: A specific business problem with measurable value
questions.explanation: Outcome alignment begins with real operational pain and a way to judge whether AI improved it.

questions.question: Name three factors besides expected value that should shape AI use-case selection.
questions.answer: Any three of technical feasibility, user receptivity, process disruption, resource requirements, and implementation effort.
questions.explanation: A valuable idea can still fail if the organization cannot build, adopt, or safely operate it.

questions.question: A team can automate either internal expense categorization or customer credit decisions. Which should it prioritize for a first pilot and why?
questions.answer: Internal expense categorization, if it has measurable value and feasible data, because it has lower disruption and failure impact than customer credit decisions.
questions.explanation: Selection weighs value together with feasibility, user impact, and risk rather than choosing only the most consequential possible automation.

questions.question: What comes after laying an AI foundation?
options: Scale every use case
Launch focused pilots
Replace all workflows
Stop measuring results
questions.answer: Launch focused pilots
questions.explanation: The sequence is foundation, pilot, then scale based on demonstrated value.

questions.question: Why separate AI transformation into stages?
questions.answer: To establish alignment and governance, learn from focused evidence, and scale only proven practices.
questions.explanation: Stages stop an organization from expanding before it has evidence and capability.

questions.question: A company has a successful chatbot demo but no usage data or training plan. What should it do before scaling?
questions.answer: Treat it as a pilot: define measurement, collect evidence, and build the needed governance and capability before a broad rollout.
questions.explanation: A demo is not enough evidence to pass from pilot to scale.

questions.question: Who should be represented on an AI steering committee?
options: Only the AI engineering team
Only executives
Business, technology, finance, legal/compliance, and executive sponsorship
Only external consultants
questions.answer: Business, technology, finance, legal/compliance, and executive sponsorship
questions.explanation: AI decisions cross operational, technical, financial, and regulatory boundaries.

questions.question: Why is a cross-functional AI steering committee needed?
questions.answer: Because AI changes work, data, risk, budgets, and accountability across multiple functions.
questions.explanation: The committee brings the authority and expertise needed to resolve those connected trade-offs.

questions.question: A proposed AI tool will process customer data and change a sales workflow. Which committee roles should evaluate it?
questions.answer: The executive sponsor, sales leader, technology leader, finance representative, and legal or compliance leader.
questions.explanation: Each role covers a material part of the decision: authority, workflow, implementation, investment, and permitted use.

questions.question: What is a change champion’s main role?
options: Approve all AI spending
Help peers adopt AI and surface workflow concerns
Replace the steering committee
Train models
questions.answer: Help peers adopt AI and surface workflow concerns
questions.explanation: Champions make change credible locally and reveal practical resistance.

questions.question: Why include constructive skeptics in a champion network?
questions.answer: Their questions expose legitimate implementation concerns.
questions.explanation: Skepticism can reveal risks and friction that enthusiasm misses.

questions.question: Adoption is weak in one team. What should a champion do?
questions.answer: Use the team’s real work in peer mentoring, gather objections, and share workable practices.
questions.explanation: Local examples and peer trust address workflow-specific friction.

questions.question: Which set best evaluates an AI pilot?
options: Cost only
Adoption, efficiency, quality, and satisfaction
Accuracy only
Executive opinion only
questions.answer: Adoption, efficiency, quality, and satisfaction
questions.explanation: Several dimensions reveal trade-offs a single metric hides.

questions.question: Why is time saved alone insufficient for a pilot scorecard?
questions.answer: The tool may save time while lowering quality or being rejected by users.
questions.explanation: The scorecard checks adoption, quality, and satisfaction alongside efficiency.

questions.question: A pilot is fast but has frequent errors. What should the scorecard decision be?
questions.answer: Do not scale yet; improve quality while checking adoption and user feedback.
questions.explanation: Efficiency cannot outweigh unacceptable output quality.

questions.question: What is a center of excellence for AI?
options: A team that centralizes reusable practices, support, and experimentation
A model-training vendor
A quarterly executive meeting
A single department’s chatbot
questions.answer: A team that centralizes reusable practices, support, and experimentation
questions.explanation: It spreads lessons across functions while retaining domain input.

questions.question: Why use rotations in an AI center of excellence?
questions.answer: To build functional expertise and keep the center connected to current business needs.
questions.explanation: Rotations prevent detached central governance.

questions.question: Two teams repeat the same AI integration mistake. What should the center do?
questions.answer: Publish a reusable practice, provide support, and share the lesson across teams.
questions.explanation: The center exists to prevent each department from relearning the same lesson.

questions.question: Which audience most needs deep technical AI training?
options: Executives
Power users and champions
Every employee equally
Only legal staff
questions.answer: Power users and champions
questions.explanation: Executives need strategy context, while power users need advanced hands-on capability.

questions.question: How should AI proficiency be validated?
questions.answer: With demonstrated performance on real work rather than attendance or recall tests.
questions.explanation: Real assessments show usable capability.

questions.question: What should a manager’s AI learning path emphasize?
questions.answer: Translating AI strategy into daily team workflows and decisions.
questions.explanation: Managers bridge executive intent and operational practice.

questions.question: What does an AI governance framework define?
options: Only model choice
Access, permitted use, quality, review, and compliance rules
Only training schedules
Only cost targets
questions.answer: Access, permitted use, quality, review, and compliance rules
questions.explanation: Governance makes safe adoption repeatable across several control areas.

questions.question: Why are explicit AI usage guidelines necessary?
questions.answer: They prevent unsafe data handling and consequential automation while allowing safe experimentation.
questions.explanation: Clear boundaries avoid both uncontrolled use and blanket prohibition.

questions.question: How should a company govern AI assistance for employment decisions?
questions.answer: Set access and data rules, require human review, define quality standards, and keep audit evidence.
questions.explanation: Employment decisions are consequential and need policy plus oversight.

questions.question: What best describes agent-centered workflow redesign?
options: Adding a chatbot to one unchanged manual step
Rebuilding an end-to-end process around agent capabilities and human judgment
Replacing every human decision with an agent
Buying a more expensive AI model
questions.answer: Rebuilding an end-to-end process around agent capabilities and human judgment
questions.explanation: The focus is the whole workflow: its handoffs, decisions, and ownership—not merely a faster isolated step.

questions.question: Why can automating one legacy workflow step fail to produce a better business outcome?
questions.answer: It can preserve the old handoffs, bottlenecks, and decision rules, making a flawed process faster without improving its result.
questions.explanation: A correct answer identifies that local automation does not repair problems elsewhere in the end-to-end process.

questions.question: A support team wants an agent to draft replies, but agents still wait for people to copy data among three systems. What redesign should the team consider?
questions.answer: Redesign the full case workflow so the agent can gather authorized context and prepare resolutions, while people retain explicit approval for sensitive or high-value decisions.
questions.explanation: This removes unnecessary handoffs and keeps human judgment at consequential decision points instead of only speeding up reply drafting.

questions.question: What does agent-ready context infrastructure provide?
options: A longer system prompt for every task
Authoritative organizational data that agents can discover, access, and use when needed
A replacement for access controls
A guarantee that agents never make mistakes
questions.answer: Authoritative organizational data that agents can discover, access, and use when needed
questions.explanation: It is the data and integration foundation that lets an agent obtain reliable context for its task.

questions.question: Why cannot a more capable model alone overcome fragmented enterprise data?
questions.answer: The model still lacks the authoritative, accessible, and connected information needed to reason and act on the task.
questions.explanation: The scoring point is that missing or poor-quality context is an infrastructure problem, not only a model-capability problem.

questions.question: A service agent can see a customer profile but not current invoices or refund policy. What should the team improve before expecting reliable resolutions?
questions.answer: Build authorized, reliable access and integration for the invoice and policy sources so the agent can assemble the required current context.
questions.explanation: The missing information should be made discoverable and usable with appropriate controls; asking the agent to infer it is unreliable.

questions.question: Which workflow is at the highest rung of the complexity ladder?
options: Summarizing one document
Drafting one email
Checking an order, applying a policy, and drafting a reply
Coordinating customer support, fulfillment, and finance across a case
questions.answer: Coordinating customer support, fulfillment, and finance across a case
questions.explanation: Cross-functional work spans teams and systems, so it has more coordination and failure modes than a bounded task or one multi-step flow.

questions.question: Why should a cross-functional agent process not be treated as a bigger chatbot task?
questions.answer: It adds coordination across systems and teams, authority decisions, integrations, and more failure and escalation paths.
questions.explanation: The essential point is that operational scope changes the kind of controls and design the workflow needs.

questions.question: An agent collects contract details, checks approved terms, routes exceptions to legal, and updates procurement. How should the team use the complexity ladder?
questions.answer: Classify it as at least a multi-stage workflow, and likely cross-functional because it spans legal and procurement; design integrations, ownership, and exception handling accordingly.
questions.explanation: The classification helps the team plan for the real coordination burden instead of treating the project as a simple drafting assistant.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of domain-expert-calibrated validation?
options: To select the cheapest model
To compare agent decisions with qualified expert judgments on representative cases
To eliminate all human review
To test only generic benchmark scores
questions.answer: To compare agent decisions with qualified expert judgments on representative cases
questions.explanation: The expert comparison establishes domain-specific ground truth for consequential work.

questions.question: Why is a generic benchmark insufficient for a high-stakes domain agent?
questions.answer: It does not establish whether the agent meets that domain's real standards for reasoning, accuracy, compliance, and risk on representative cases.
questions.explanation: A complete answer contrasts generic scores with domain-specific expert ground truth.

questions.question: A fraud agent matches experts on 96% of cases but misses a rare, severe fraud pattern. What should the validation team do?
questions.answer: Treat the severe miss as a domain risk to investigate and include in the acceptance criteria, rather than accepting the agent on its average alignment score alone.
questions.explanation: Representative validation must account for harmful edge cases and domain risk, not only aggregate agreement.

questions.question: What must an enterprise delegation operating model define besides the task assigned to an agent?
options: Only the model provider
Human accountability, escalation points, and autonomy limits
A new chat interface
Unlimited access to all systems
questions.answer: Human accountability, escalation points, and autonomy limits
questions.explanation: Delegation transfers work, not responsibility; the operating model makes ownership and boundaries explicit.

questions.question: Why is delegation not merely an interface change from chat to automation?
questions.answer: It changes who monitors work, resolves ambiguity, accepts output, and owns failures, so those responsibilities must be designed explicitly.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is organizational accountability, not only the user interface.

questions.question: An onboarding agent can create accounts and change payroll details. How should the company set its delegation model?
questions.answer: Allow routine account setup within defined access limits, assign a human owner for each case, and require escalation and explicit approval for payroll changes or missing evidence.
questions.explanation: A good model defines routine autonomy, accountable ownership, and checkpoints for consequential exceptions.

questions.question: What do human-agent work redesign metrics measure beyond hours saved?
options: Only model latency
Whether people move toward higher-leverage work such as judgment, relationships, and learning
Only number of agent messages
Only software license cost
questions.answer: Whether people move toward higher-leverage work such as judgment, relationships, and learning
questions.explanation: The metrics evaluate how automation changes the composition and developmental value of human work.

questions.question: Why can a time-saved metric be misleading after automation?
questions.answer: Saved time may be consumed by reviewing errors and handling exceptions instead of valuable judgment, relationships, or learning.
questions.explanation: A correct answer identifies the hidden burden that a simple efficiency measure can miss.

questions.question: A support agent cuts reply time in half, but staff now spend the saved time correcting its responses. What should the team conclude?
questions.answer: The efficiency gain has not yet created the intended higher-leverage capacity; measure correction and exception work and improve the workflow before calling the redesign successful.
questions.explanation: Work-composition metrics reveal whether apparent speed actually improves the team's work.

questions.question: What does a hybrid agent build strategy recommend?
options: Build every component from scratch
Use only packaged agents
Use packaged capabilities where they fit and customize where proprietary needs create material value
Avoid governance for bought components
questions.answer: Use packaged capabilities where they fit and customize where proprietary needs create material value
questions.explanation: The strategy balances speed from packaged components with targeted custom investment for differentiation.

questions.question: Why is a fully custom agent strategy often a poor default?
questions.answer: It requires sustained engineering investment even for common capabilities where a packaged solution may already work well.
questions.explanation: The key trade-off is control and differentiation versus the cost of building and maintaining everything yourself.

questions.question: A company needs meeting summaries and a pricing workflow tied to proprietary contracts and margin rules. Which parts should it consider customizing?
questions.answer: Use a packaged capability for meeting summaries and consider a custom component for pricing, where proprietary rules and differentiation justify the engineering cost.
questions.explanation: The strategy directs custom work to the part where generic products are least likely to fit the distinctive workflow.

questions.question: Which control prevents an agent from continuing indefinitely even if it never declares completion?
options: A hard step or cost limit
A longer system prompt
A larger context window
A more detailed final answer
questions.answer: A hard step or cost limit
questions.explanation: A hard operational limit ends the run independently of the model's completion judgment.

questions.question: Why is a model-declared final answer not always enough to terminate an agent safely?
questions.answer: The model can stop too early or be wrong, so hard limits and, when needed, goal verification provide independent boundaries.
questions.explanation: A correct answer identifies both premature completion risk and an independent termination safeguard.

questions.question: An agent has retried a deployment check 20 times without passing. What should its termination policy do?
questions.answer: Stop at the configured retry or step limit, preserve the evidence gathered, and escalate or report the incomplete result instead of retrying indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The policy bounds waste and makes incomplete work visible for a human or a later recovery path.

questions.question: What does an artifact-based handoff give the receiving agent?
options: A typed, inspectable deliverable
The full prior conversation
All of the sender's tool credentials
An unstructured stream of thoughts
questions.answer: A typed, inspectable deliverable
questions.explanation: The handoff is a defined result, such as a plan or test report, rather than raw conversation history.

questions.question: Why are typed artifacts preferable to raw transcripts for many agent handoffs?
questions.answer: They define the handoff contract, remove irrelevant reasoning, and make the result inspectable and auditable.
questions.explanation: A correct answer covers both clearer context for the receiver and better operational traceability.

questions.question: A coding agent receives a 200-message research chat and misses a requirement. How should the workflow change?
questions.answer: Have the research agent produce a validated requirements artifact and pass that artifact to the coding agent instead of the full chat.
questions.explanation: The explicit artifact gives the coding agent a focused, reviewable contract for implementation.

questions.question: What makes an agent cognitive state bounded?
options: Its schema fields have fixed size limits
It stores every prior message
It never stores decisions
It uses a larger context window
questions.answer: Its schema fields have fixed size limits
questions.explanation: A bounded state limits fields such as facts, decisions, and next actions, requiring deliberate retention and eviction.

questions.question: What is the main risk of a poorly designed bounded-state schema?
questions.answer: It can omit or evict information that the agent cannot reconstruct later.
questions.explanation: The fixed-size approach controls growth, but its schema determines what can survive between turns.

questions.question: A long-running agent keeps rereading a massive transcript and forgets past decisions. What change best applies this concept?
questions.answer: Persist a small schema with the current goal, constraints, key facts, decisions, artifacts, questions, and next actions, updating it each turn within fixed limits.
questions.explanation: The fixed state preserves decision-relevant information without treating the full transcript as persistent memory.

questions.question: What can code-as-action express that a single structured tool call usually cannot?
options: Variables, branches, loops, and several tool calls
A tool schema
A final answer
A user identity
questions.answer: Variables, branches, loops, and several tool calls
questions.explanation: The executable action can compose tools with ordinary program control flow in one sandboxed step.

questions.question: Why does code-as-action require stronger controls than a single typed tool call?
questions.answer: Generated code can combine broader control flow and multiple side effects, making it harder to audit and more dangerous if it is untrusted.
questions.explanation: The key trade-off is greater expressiveness versus reduced auditability and a larger execution risk.

questions.question: An agent must query three approved APIs, filter results, and retry one temporary error. Which execution design fits, and what guardrail is essential?
questions.answer: Use a code-as-action step for the composed workflow, but run it in an isolated sandbox with only the required scoped API access.
questions.explanation: Code gives the workflow compact control flow; isolation and least privilege contain the broader execution capability.

questions.question: When can context rot begin?
options: Before the context window is full
Only after the context window overflows
Only after a tool error
Only in multi-agent systems
questions.answer: Before the context window is full
questions.explanation: Context quality can degrade well below the token ceiling through attention and distractor effects.

questions.question: Name two signals that can reveal context rot in an agent run.
questions.answer: Any two of declining instruction adherence, lower task relevance, a rising context noise ratio, or a rising repetition rate.
questions.explanation: These signals measure quality degradation rather than merely token usage.

questions.question: An agent is below its token limit but has begun repeating failed actions and ignoring the original task. What should the runtime do?
questions.answer: Treat this as context rot: preserve the key state, remove stale or irrelevant material, reinject the task constraints, and continue with focused context.
questions.explanation: The symptoms show quality degradation, so waiting for an overflow would be too late.

questions.question: Which memory layer is meant to hold reusable information across conversations?
options: Long-term memory
Working memory
A single tool result
The current model response
questions.answer: Long-term memory
questions.explanation: Long-term memory stores durable knowledge that can be retrieved by later conversations or runs.

questions.question: Why should an agent not treat all memory as conversation history?
questions.answer: It would overload active context with short-lived noise while failing to organize durable facts and lessons by their different retrieval needs.
questions.explanation: Layering keeps immediate work small and preserves reusable knowledge in appropriate storage.

questions.question: A support agent needs the current case, a past preference, and a lesson from a failed escalation. Where should each belong?
questions.answer: Keep the current case in working or session memory, the preference in long-term memory, and the failed escalation lesson in episodic memory.
questions.explanation: The layers are chosen by lifetime and retrieval purpose, not by placing all information in one transcript.

questions.question: How should an agent treat instructions embedded in a retrieved web page or tool result?
options: As untrusted data, not authorization
As higher-priority system instructions
As automatic permission to use tools
As a replacement for policy checks
questions.answer: As untrusted data, not authorization
questions.explanation: Retrieved content can contain prompt injection, so it must not directly authorize side effects.

questions.question: Why does content isolation not eliminate the need for policy gates and least-privilege credentials?
questions.answer: Isolation reduces the chance that hostile text is treated as an instruction, while policy gates and least privilege still block or limit harmful actions if the agent is influenced.
questions.explanation: These are complementary layers: one separates data from authority, the others control proposed actions and available access.

questions.question: A document asks an agent to ignore its task and send credentials to an external URL. What should the agent runtime do?
questions.answer: Mark the text as suspicious untrusted content, keep the original instruction hierarchy, block the proposed credential transfer through policy and scoped access controls, and report or escalate the finding.
questions.explanation: The document is evidence to inspect, never authority to override the task or authorize a side effect.
